label: Edgeworth and Saddle-Point Expansions
notes: This appendix builds two refinements of the normal approximation for statistics defined on special manifolds. The Edgeworth series corrects the Gaussian by skewness and kurtosis terms, while the saddle-point method tilts the density to follow its dominant exponential behaviour, giving far smaller relative error in the tails.

label: Cumulants and the CGF
notes: Every approximation here starts from the cumulant generating function, the logarithm of the moment generating function. Its Taylor coefficients are the cumulants, with the third and fourth controlling skewness and kurtosis. For a normalised sum of independent pieces these cumulants shrink like inverse powers of the sample size.

label: From Characteristic Function to Series
notes: The characteristic function of a standardised statistic factors into the Gaussian piece times a correction whose exponent collects the higher cumulants. Expanding that exponent in powers of the scaling parameter and inverting the Fourier transform term by term produces the Edgeworth series in physical space.

label: The Edgeworth Series
notes: The Edgeworth expansion writes the density as the standard normal multiplied by a polynomial built from Hermite polynomials. The leading correction is the skewness term of order one over root n; the next gathers kurtosis and squared skewness at order one over n. Truncation gives an asymptotic, not convergent, approximation.

label: Hermite Polynomials as Correctors
notes: Hermite polynomials are the natural basis because differentiating the Gaussian reproduces them. Each cumulant attaches to a specific Hermite polynomial, so the third cumulant multiplies the degree-three Hermite term and bends the curve asymmetrically. The visual shows how this single term shifts mass to correct skew.

label: Density, Normal, and Correction
notes: Here the true skewed density, its plain normal approximation, and the Edgeworth-corrected curve are overlaid. The normal sits symmetric and misses the lean; the corrected curve thickens one shoulder and thins the other, tracking the true density much more closely through the body of the distribution.

label: The Saddle-Point Idea
notes: The saddle-point method recovers the density by inverse Laplace transform and deforms the integration contour through the point where the exponent is stationary. That saddle lies on the real axis at the value solving the tilt equation, and the integrand decays steeply away from it, concentrating all the mass there.

label: Steepest Descent Contour
notes: This diagram shows the complex plane with level curves of the exponent and the steepest-descent path bending through the saddle on the real axis. Along that path the exponent is real and maximal at the saddle, so a local Gaussian fit to the contour yields the leading saddle-point density estimate.

label: Exponential Tilt and Legendre
notes: Evaluating at the saddle is an exponential tilt: the distribution is re-centred so the point of interest becomes its mean. The exponent of the approximation is the Legendre transform of the cumulant function, the same convex conjugate that governs large-deviation rates and dually flat geometry on these manifolds.

label: Relative Error in the Tails
notes: The saddle-point density carries a relative error of order one over n that stays uniform into the tails, whereas the Edgeworth series controls only absolute error and can turn negative far out. This tail accuracy is exactly what manifold inference needs when test statistics reach extreme values.

label: Statistics on Special Manifolds
notes: On Stiefel and Grassmann manifolds the cumulants of invariant statistics come from matrix moments of the underlying distribution. Feeding those cumulants into either expansion yields tractable densities for test statistics, so the abstract machinery becomes a concrete recipe for p-values and confidence regions on the manifold.

label: Summary and Checks
notes: To summarise: cumulants drive both methods; Edgeworth adds Hermite corrections for the body, saddle-point tilts the density for the tails, and the Legendre transform links them. A good numerical check confirms the corrected density integrates near one and beats the plain normal in total variation.
